2.text: eating with others, from the same dish, will try by an incantation to make

3.text: the motions of his rivals slower than his own. Women apply incantations

4.text: to their sinew-thread in order to make it stronger. A man who has forgotten

5.text: a magic formula will resort to another incantation which is helpful in recalling

6.text: to one’s mind things which are forgotten.

7.text: A number of incantations relate to matters of love. Those referring to

8.text: birth, death, and funeral-rites, will be treated in a separate chapter. A large

9.text: proportion of incantations refer to the cure of diseases. As may be seen

10.text: from this enumeration, incantations are usually benevolent in their purport

11.text: toward man. In this they are at variance with another series of magic acts,

12.text: which always portend harm to some one.

13.text: These latter are called in Chukchee uiˊwel. Most of them are supposed
13.note: {ui'wel} is below the two-page floor in lexicon lookup, no key returned; raised mark defaults to stress per keying_spec.md §4 (“Read every raised mark as stress (U+02CA) by default”), keyed manually as uiˊwel.

14.text: to have a capricious material shape created for them by the person performing

15.text: the incantation. They may be animals, monsters, or even inanimate objects.

16.text: In this shape they are sent to the person “doomed to anger,” to lure him

17.text: in some way to danger and destruction. After that they come back, and are

18.text: themselves destroyed, or simply disintegrate on the spot. I call them “spells,”

19.text: in the absence of any more adequate word.

20.text: Conformably with this difference between incantations and “spells,” the

21.text: “Old Women of the Time of the First Creation,” mentioned in several

22.text: formulas, are there called also “Women of Incantation,” signifying that their

23.text: performance is beneficent to the applicant. The small old woman of Keˊrek
23.as_typed: performance is beneficent to the applicant. The small old woman of {Ke'rek}

24.text: stock, mentioned in the tale of the Scabby Shaman,¹ who did much harm to
24.note: footnote marker keyed as superscript ¹ (U+00B9) per keying_spec.md §2.10; mz/ocr draft showed a plain “l”.

25.text: the hero of the tale, is called, on the contrary, an “Old Woman of Spells.”

26.text: There are, however, several branches of incantations which are also harmful

27.text: in their purpose. These are called “Spell Incantation” (oiwaˊčirg̣-êˊwgan) or

28.text: “Anger Incantation” (aˊnñêna-êˊwgan). Of these I shall speak later on.

29.text: Some of the incantations have a very short formula, consisting often of

30.text: but a few words. Others are more elaborate, and are directed to various

31.text: stars and “Beings,” with an application to every one for some spirit assistance.

32.text: Many of them are contrived in the form of a dialogue between the performer

33.text: and the powers to whom application is made.

34.text: Incantations may be inherited from parents, who, dying or growing old,

35.text: transfer to their heirs their spiritual as well as their material property. Or

36.text: they may be received in dreams from various vaˊɪrg̣ɪt or keˊlet, or may even
36.note: {va'irgit} → vaˊɪrg̣ɪt, {ke'let} → keˊlet, both ratified lexicon keys; dot-below-g confirmed at 4× in va'ɪrg̣ɪt.
36.as_typed: they may be received in dreams from various {va'i_rg.i_t} or {ke'let}, or may even

37.text: be bought from competent persons. These are, of course, mostly shamans;

38.text: but, besides the shamans, there are also those who know a great many

39.text: incantations, and, moreover, know how to apply them, and who, therefore,

40.text: are able to give advice and assistance in various cases of trouble. Such

41.text: persons are called the “knowing ones” (hiuleˊt-reˊmkɪn, “knowing people”).
